title: Two in Every Classroom
author: Simon Pollard
summary: Simon Pollard, a primary educator of more than thirty years, writes about discovering how little he knew about Developmental Language Disorder after a walk with his daughter, a newly qualified speech and language therapist. He reports that nearly 70 percent of UK teachers surveyed had never heard of DLD or knew little about it, even though it affects around two children in every class of 30. DLD is lifelong, has no known cause, and can be missed or mistaken for poor behaviour, poor listening or inattention. He recalls a Year 4 child he judged to be ignoring him who was actually still processing a three-step instruction. Citing Speech and Language UK reports, he notes that 78 percent of teachers say children who struggle with language are being punished for it, and that there is no agreed national pathway for identification. His practical takeaway is that helpful strategies are mostly good teaching made deliberate, such as explicit vocabulary teaching, checking understanding and using visuals, and that speech and language therapists belong at the table.
points: DLD affects roughly two in every class of 30, yet most teachers have never heard of it or know little about it.
DLD hides in plain sight and is easily misread as poor behaviour, poor listening or inattention, and it often overlaps with dyslexia.
Many teachers report that children who struggle with language are punished for it, which makes recognition an equity issue.
Strategies that help children with DLD, such as explicit vocabulary and checking understanding, help every child, so this is inclusion rather than an add-on.
Speech and language therapists should have a seat in school networks because there is no agreed national pathway for identifying DLD.
quotes: In a YouGov survey for Speech and Language UK, nearly 70% of teachers said they had either never heard of DLD or didn’t know much about it.
That matters, because DLD isn’t rare. It affects around 7.5% of children: roughly two in every class of 30.
DLD can be missed, misdiagnosed, or mistaken for poor behaviour, poor listening or inattention.
What they were actually doing was still processing the three-step instruction I had just given them.
In Speech and Language UK’s Support not sanctions report, 78% of teachers surveyed said that children who struggle with talking and understanding words are being punished because of it.
I noticed when the teachers would be talking, it would be like a wall up – like I couldn’t hear anything.

The good news is that what helps children with DLD is mostly good teaching, made deliberate. RADLD’s guidance for schools includes teaching vocabulary explicitly, checking understanding by asking questions, and using visuals to make content stand out.
